prompt: Why is texting while driving especially dangerous?
choices: It is only risky at highway speeds
It only distracts you while you type, not while you read
It takes your eyes, your hands, and your mind off driving at the same time
It is only risky for drivers who text slowly
explanation: Texting combines all three kinds of distraction: visual (eyes off the road), manual (hands off the wheel) and cognitive (mind off driving). Reading a message is just as distracting as typing one.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 94, PA p. 36, TX p. 60)

prompt: Which type of distraction takes your eyes off the road?
choices: Visual
Manual
Cognitive
Mechanical
explanation: A visual distraction is any task that takes your eyes off the road, such as looking at a phone or a billboard. Manual distractions take your hands off the wheel, and cognitive distractions take your mind off driving.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 94, PA p. 36)

prompt: Daydreaming or thinking hard about a problem while you drive is an example of which type of distraction?
choices: Visual
Manual
None, as long as your eyes are on the road
Cognitive
explanation: A cognitive distraction takes your mind off driving even when your eyes are on the road and your hands are on the wheel. Handbooks warn that mental activities are just as dangerous as looking away.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 94, TX p. 60, NY p. 45)

prompt: Why can a hands-free phone call still be dangerous while driving?
choices: It is not dangerous; only handheld phones distract drivers
It takes your attention off driving, even with your eyes on the road
It is only dangerous for drivers under 18
It is only dangerous if the call is longer than an hour
explanation: A phone conversation is a cognitive distraction whether or not you hold the phone. Handbooks list talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, as a distraction that slows your reactions.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 36, NJ p. 94)

prompt: Your phone rings while you are driving. What is the safest choice?
choices: Answer quickly and keep the call short
Let it go to voicemail, and pull safely off the road if you must call back
Check who is calling while you wait at the next red light
Hold the phone low in your lap so you can still see the road
explanation: Do not answer while driving. If you must return or make a call, first pull safely off the road, or have a passenger make the call for you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 76, TX p. 60)

prompt: When is the best time to enter a destination into your navigation system?
choices: While driving slowly in a parking lot exit
While stopped at a stop sign
On the highway when traffic is light
Before you start driving
explanation: Plan your route and set up the navigation system before you move. Programming a GPS while the vehicle is moving takes your eyes, hands and attention off driving.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 60, NJ p. 94, AK p. 29)

prompt: Your young child in the back seat is upset and needs help while you are driving. What should you do?
choices: Pull over to a safe place, then help the child
Reach back to help while watching the road in the mirror
Turn around to help each time you stop at a light
Speed up so you get to your destination sooner
explanation: Do not try to handle children while driving. Pull over to a safe location to deal with distracting or urgent situations.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NE p. 72, AK p. 29, CO p. 9)

prompt: What is the safest way to bring a dog along on a drive?
choices: Let it sit on your lap so it stays calm
Let it move freely around the back seat
Secure it in a pet carrier, kennel, or pet harness
Let it ride in the front seat with its head out the window
explanation: A loose pet is a dangerous distraction and can be thrown around in a crash. Secure pets in a carrier, portable kennel or pet harness, and never let a pet sit on your lap while you drive.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NE p. 72, NY p. 45, AK p. 29)

prompt: On a mild, sunny day, is it safe to leave a pet in a parked car with the windows up for "just a few minutes"?
choices: Yes, as long as the outside temperature is mild
Yes, if you ran the air conditioning right before parking
Yes, if the car is parked in partial shade
No, the temperature inside a parked car can rise quickly to dangerous levels
explanation: The inside of a parked car heats up fast, even when the outside temperature is mild. Never leave children or pets unattended in a vehicle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 73, NE p. 34)

prompt: You are passing a crash scene on the other side of the highway. What should you do?
choices: Slow down sharply to see what happened
Keep your attention on driving and avoid staring at the scene
Take a quick photo to share with others
Drift toward the center line to get a better view
explanation: "Rubbernecking" at a crash or work zone is a visual and mental distraction that can cause another crash. Keep your eyes on your own lane and the traffic around you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 36, CO p. 9)

prompt: The car ahead of you keeps drifting within its lane and changing speed for no clear reason. What is the best response?
choices: Pass it closely and quickly to get away from it
Follow closely so the driver notices you in the mirror
Give it extra room and be very careful about passing it
Hold your horn down until the driver pulls over
explanation: Drifting and uneven speed are signs of a distracted driver who may not know you are there. Keep a safe following distance and take extra care when passing, since the driver may drift in front of you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 60)

prompt: Why might a driver deep in a phone conversation fail to notice a red light right in front of them?
choices: Your eyes can look at something without your mind really seeing it when your attention is elsewhere
Phone signals interfere with the color of traffic lights
Phone calls only affect hearing, not seeing
It only happens to drivers who need glasses
explanation: Handbooks warn that your eyes can gaze at objects in the driving scene but fail to see them because your attention is somewhere else. This is why mental distractions are so dangerous.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 60, NY p. 45)

prompt: A passenger starts a heated argument with you while you are driving in heavy traffic. What should you do?
choices: Put off the discussion until you are stopped somewhere safe
Turn toward the passenger so you can talk it through
Drive faster to end the trip sooner
Keep arguing but grip the wheel tighter
explanation: Emotionally intense conversations are a cognitive distraction. Handbooks advise avoiding arguments while driving and holding them in a safe place instead.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 45, TX p. 60, NE p. 72)

prompt: At highway speed, looking away from the road for just a few seconds can mean traveling about how far without watching where you are going?
choices: About one car length
About 10 feet
The length of a football field
The width of a single lane
explanation: Even a few seconds of inattention at highway speed can mean traveling the length of a football field blind. A short glance at a phone covers a long distance.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 94)

prompt: What is the only real cure for being drowsy behind the wheel?
choices: Turning up the radio
Sleep
Opening the windows for cold air
Chewing gum
explanation: Rest is the only safe remedy for drowsiness. Radio, open windows and similar tricks do not prevent you from falling asleep.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 61, NY p. 52, PA p. 37)

prompt: Which of these is a warning sign that you are too drowsy to drive safely?
choices: You are checking your mirrors often
Your hands feel warm on the steering wheel
You notice signs for an upcoming rest area
You can't remember driving the last few miles
explanation: Warning signs of drowsy driving include not remembering the last few miles, frequent yawning, heavy eyelids, drifting out of your lane and hitting rumble strips.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 51)

prompt: On a long night drive you keep yawning, and you just drifted onto the rumble strip. What is the best thing to do?
choices: Turn the air conditioning to cold and keep going
Speed up to reach your destination sooner
Pull off at a safe place away from traffic and rest or take a nap
Drink a coffee and keep driving right away
explanation: Hitting rumble strips and constant yawning mean you are close to falling asleep. Stop in a safe place and rest. Caffeine takes time to work and does not replace sleep.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 51-52, PA p. 37)

prompt: How does caffeine affect a drowsy driver?
choices: It may help you stay alert for a short time, but it does not replace sleep
It completely cures drowsiness
It works the moment you drink it
It makes it safe to drive all night
explanation: Caffeine can promote short-term alertness, and it takes time to reach your bloodstream. Only sleep actually fixes drowsiness.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 52, TX p. 61)

prompt: Which plan best lowers the risk of drowsy driving on a long road trip?
choices: Leave right after a late night out so the roads are empty
Drive straight through without stopping to finish sooner
Do most of the driving during the hours you usually sleep
Get a full night's sleep, plan regular breaks, and share the driving with a companion
explanation: Before a long trip, get enough sleep, schedule regular rest stops and drive with a companion if you can. Driving through the night or at times you would normally be asleep raises the risk.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 52, AZ p. 61)

prompt: After hours on a straight, monotonous highway, you feel like you are in a trance. What helps prevent this "highway hypnosis"?
choices: Stare at the center of the lane ahead to stay focused
Keep your eyes moving by scanning ahead and checking mirrors, and take breaks
Turn on cruise control so you can relax your attention
Move to the left lane to make the drive more interesting
explanation: Highway hypnosis is a drowsy, trance-like state caused by monotony. Avoid fixing your eyes on one spot: scan the road, check mirrors and gauges, and stop for rest.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 94, AZ p. 61)

prompt: Why is it risky to keep driving "just a few more miles" when you are very sleepy?
choices: Feeling sleepy always passes after a few minutes
You can fall asleep for a few seconds without realizing it, and that is enough to crash
You can always feel yourself about to fall asleep in time to stop
Sleepiness only affects you after midnight
explanation: If you are tired enough, you may fall asleep and never know it, and you cannot predict when sleep will come. A few seconds asleep at the wheel can kill you.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 37, NY p. 52)

prompt: How should a lap and shoulder belt be worn?
choices: Lap belt across the stomach; shoulder belt under the arm
Lap belt loose; shoulder belt behind the back for comfort
Lap belt high on the waist; shoulder belt against the neck
Lap belt snug and low across the hips; shoulder belt across the chest and shoulder
explanation: Wear the lap belt snug and low across your hips and the shoulder belt across your shoulder and chest with little slack. Never put the shoulder belt under your arm or behind your back.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 71, PA p. 95, NJ p. 43)

prompt: A passenger tucks the shoulder belt behind his back because it rubs his neck. Why is this unsafe?
choices: His upper body and head can be thrown forward in a crash with nothing to hold them back
It is safe as long as the lap belt is fastened
It only matters in rear-end crashes
It just makes the belt wear out faster
explanation: A lap belt alone does not stop your head and chest from hitting the dashboard, steering wheel or windshield. The shoulder belt must cross the shoulder and chest, never behind the back or under the arm.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 71, AK p. 25)

prompt: How should a pregnant driver wear her seat belt?
choices: Lap belt across the middle of the belly
Shoulder belt only, with the lap belt left off
Lap belt as low as possible under the belly, shoulder belt across the chest and to the side of the belly
No belt, relying on the airbag instead
explanation: Pregnant drivers and passengers should still wear both parts of the belt. The lap belt goes low, under the abdomen, and the shoulder belt crosses the chest to the side of the belly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 71, NJ p. 43)

prompt: Your car has an automatic shoulder belt that moves into place by itself, plus a separate lap belt. What should you do?
choices: Nothing; the automatic shoulder belt is enough
Unhook the shoulder belt and use only the lap belt
Buckle the lap belt only on the highway
Buckle the lap belt too
explanation: With a two-part belt system, wear both parts. Using only the shoulder belt can let you slide out underneath it in a crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AZ p. 20, MT p. 29, NM p. 6)

prompt: Do airbags replace the need to wear a seat belt?
choices: Yes, for people in the front seats
No, airbags are designed to work together with seat belts
Yes, if the car also has side airbags
Yes, in low-speed crashes
explanation: Airbags are meant to work with seat belts, not replace them. The combination of a seat belt and an airbag gives the most protection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 49, NJ p. 43)

prompt: A friend says it is safer to be thrown clear of a crash than to be trapped by a seat belt. What is correct?
choices: Your friend is right whenever a crash involves fire or water
Your friend is right at speeds under 30 mph
Being thrown from the vehicle greatly increases your chance of being killed, so stay buckled
It depends on whether the car has airbags
explanation: Your chance of being killed is far greater if you are thrown from the vehicle. Even in rare fire or underwater crashes, a belted person is more likely to stay conscious and escape.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 25, PA p. 36)

prompt: Can a belted adult safely hold a baby on their lap in a moving car?
choices: No, crash forces make the baby impossible to hold, and the adult could crush the baby
Yes, as long as the adult is wearing a seat belt
Yes, for short trips close to home
Yes, if the adult sits in the back seat
explanation: In even a moderate crash, a baby's weight multiplies many times, and no one can hold on. An adult can also be thrown into the child. Children need a proper child restraint.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., AK p. 26)

prompt: Who in the vehicle should be buckled up?
choices: Everyone, in every seat, on every trip
Only the driver and the front-seat passenger
Only people riding on the highway
Only children
explanation: Make sure everyone is buckled up with a seat belt or proper child restraint on every trip, front seat and back.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 46, PA p. 35)

prompt: How far should you sit from the steering wheel airbag?
choices: At least 3 inches
About 6 inches
At least 10 inches, from the center of your chest to the center of the wheel
As close as possible for better control
explanation: Sit with at least 10 inches between your breastbone and the center of the steering wheel. An airbag inflates with great force and can injure someone who sits too close.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 73, NY p. 49, PA p. 95, NJ p. 46)

prompt: Where should an infant in a rear-facing child seat NEVER ride?
choices: In the back seat behind the driver
In the front seat, in front of an active passenger airbag
In the middle of the back seat
In the back seat behind the front passenger
explanation: Never put a rear-facing child seat in front of an active passenger airbag. A deploying airbag strikes the back of the child seat close to the baby's head.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 49, PA p. 95, NJ p. 46)

prompt: Where is it recommended that children 12 and under ride?
choices: In the front seat, so the driver can watch them
In the front seat, as long as the airbag is on
Anywhere, as long as they wear a lap belt
In the back seat, properly restrained
explanation: Children 12 and under should ride in the back seat. Most crashes are frontal, and a child in front can be badly hurt by a deploying airbag.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 95, NJ p. 46)

prompt: Why are children safer in the back seat of a car that has a front passenger airbag?
choices: Back seats have stronger seat belts
Airbags never deploy in crashes involving children
Most crashes are frontal, and children who sit or lean close to the airbag can be seriously injured when it deploys
The back seat is the only place a child seat fits
explanation: The back seat keeps children farther from the point of impact in frontal crashes. Children also fidget and can end up too close to the airbag compartment.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 95, NJ p. 46)

prompt: A short driver has to sit close to the steering wheel to reach the pedals. What is the recommended approach?
choices: Move the seat back as far as possible while still reaching the controls, and ask the dealer or manufacturer if 10 inches is not possible
Sit as close to the wheel as possible for better control
Pull the airbag fuse so it cannot deploy
Tilt the steering wheel up so it points at the face
explanation: Sit as far back as you can while still safely reaching the pedals and controls. If you cannot keep 10 inches from the airbag, the dealer or manufacturer may suggest other options.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 73, PA p. 95)

prompt: Which hand positions are recommended on the steering wheel for normal driving?
choices: One hand at 12 o'clock
10 and 2 o'clock with thumbs hooked inside the rim
One hand at 6 o'clock
9 and 3 o'clock or 8 and 4 o'clock
explanation: Hold the wheel at 9 and 3 or 8 and 4 o'clock, with thumbs along the face of the wheel. These positions give good control and lower the risk of injury if the airbag deploys.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 65, CA p. 15, NJ p. 53)

prompt: Why do handbooks recommend holding the wheel at 9 and 3 or 8 and 4 rather than higher on the wheel?
choices: It makes the horn easier to reach
A deploying airbag is less likely to throw your hands and arms into your face
It lets you spin the wheel faster in parking lots
It keeps your arms out of the driver's view of the gauges
explanation: With your hands lower on the wheel, an inflating airbag is less likely to force your arms back into your face. These positions also reduce over-steering and arm fatigue.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 65, NJ p. 53, NY p. 49)

prompt: When using hand-to-hand (push-pull) steering, what is the key rule?
choices: You steer with one hand at the 12 o'clock position
Your hands do not cross over each other
You cross one arm over the other at the top of the wheel
You grip the inside of the rim with your palm facing in
explanation: In push-pull steering, one hand pushes the wheel up while the other slides and pulls down, so your hands never cross over the middle of the wheel.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 15, PA p. 65)

prompt: Another driver cuts you off and then makes an angry gesture. What should you do?
choices: Gesture back so they know they were wrong
Speed up and pull alongside to confront them
Follow closely to show them how it feels
Ignore it, avoid eye contact, and give the driver room
explanation: Never take it personally or retaliate. Avoid eye contact, ignore gestures and do not return them, and move away from the aggressive driver.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 46, PA p. 64)

prompt: An angry driver has followed you for several miles after a traffic dispute. Where should you go?
choices: To a police station or a busy public place where you can get help
Straight home so you can get inside and lock the door
Onto a quiet side road to talk it out
To the shoulder, then get out to photograph their plate
explanation: If an aggressive driver follows you, do not go home and do not stop and get out. Drive to a police station or another place with people who can help.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 64, NY p. 46)

prompt: A driver behind you is tailgating and flashing their lights because they want to pass. What is the best response?
choices: Tap your brakes so they back off
Speed up so they can't get around you
Let them pass when it is safe, without speeding up or braking suddenly
Pace the car next to you so they can't pass
explanation: Do not challenge an aggressive driver. If someone demands to pass, let them go. Speeding up, blocking or brake-checking only raises the danger.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 64, TX p. 72, NY p. 46)

prompt: You often feel rushed and angry in traffic on your way to work. Which habit best helps prevent aggressive driving?
choices: Drive faster to make up time when the road clears
Use your horn to keep slow traffic moving
Switch lanes whenever another lane looks faster
Leave earlier and allow extra time for delays
explanation: Planning ahead and allowing extra travel time for traffic, construction or crashes helps you stay calm. Rushing leads to speeding, tailgating and risky lane changes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 72, NY p. 46)

prompt: What is the difference between aggressive driving and road rage?
choices: They are two names for the same thing
Aggressive driving usually breaks traffic laws; road rage is an angry, hostile act meant to provoke, threaten, or harm others
Road rage only means honking too much
Aggressive driving is a crime, but road rage is only rude
explanation: Aggressive driving, such as speeding, tailgating and unsafe lane changes, generally breaks traffic laws. It can grow into road rage, an angry, hostile state that can lead to threats or violence and break criminal laws.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NY p. 46, NJ p. 92)

prompt: You just got upsetting news and feel very angry. What should you do before driving?
choices: Drive right away, since focusing on the road will calm you
Drive faster to get somewhere you can relax
Take time to calm down, or let someone else drive
Turn the music up loud and start driving
explanation: Strong emotions such as anger, worry or excitement affect your judgment and reactions. Take time to cool off before you drive, or have someone else drive.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 92, NY p. 46, CO p. 9)

prompt: Where should you find the correct air pressure for your car's tires?
choices: On the label on the driver's door jamb or in the owner's manual
The maximum pressure printed on the tire sidewall
The default setting on a gas station air pump
Whatever pressure makes the tires look full
explanation: Use the pressure listed on the driver's door jamb or in the owner's manual. A tire can be underinflated without looking low, so check it with a gauge.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 48, PA p. 35)

prompt: When is the best time to check your tire pressure?
choices: When the tires are cold, before driving or after the car has sat for a while
Right after a long highway drive
Only when a tire looks flat
Only once a year
explanation: Check tire pressure when the tires are cold. Driving warms the air inside, which raises the reading and can hide underinflation.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NJ p. 48, PA p. 35)

prompt: How do worn or bald tires affect your driving?
choices: They grip better in rain because more rubber touches the road
They only affect fuel economy
They increase stopping distance and the risk of hydroplaning
They make no difference unless a tire goes flat
explanation: Worn tires increase stopping distance, make turning harder, raise the risk of hydroplaning on wet roads and are more likely to go flat.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 9, NJ p. 48)

prompt: Your steering wheel shakes and the car pulls to one side. What should you do?
choices: Ignore it unless it gets worse
Have a mechanic check the tires, wheels, and steering
Grip the wheel harder and keep driving as usual
Let some air out of all four tires
explanation: A shaking wheel or a vehicle that pulls to one side can mean tire, wheel balance or steering problems. Have a mechanic check it before it causes a breakdown or crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 9, NJ p. 48)

prompt: Your windshield wipers leave streaks and smears when it rains. What should you do?
choices: Turn the defroster to high instead
Use the wipers only on the highway
Wait until they stop working completely
Replace the wiper blades
explanation: Wipers must keep rain and snow off the windshield so you can see. If the blades are not working well, replace them, and keep the washer fluid full.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 9)

prompt: You hear a loud rumble from under the car and smell exhaust inside. Why should you get it fixed right away?
choices: It means the engine is low on oil
It only affects fuel economy
A leaking exhaust system can let deadly carbon monoxide into the car
It means the tires are underinflated
explanation: Fumes from a leaky exhaust system can kill in a very short time. Most exhaust problems can be heard, so have them repaired promptly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 9, TX p. 74)

prompt: In what order should you adjust the seat and mirrors before driving?
choices: Adjust the seat first, then the mirrors
Adjust the mirrors first, then the seat
Adjust the mirrors while driving
Adjust the seat only; mirrors never need changing
explanation: Set your mirrors after you adjust your seat, since moving the seat changes your view. Mirrors may need adjusting for each driver.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 35, CO p. 9)

prompt: Where should your head restraint be adjusted?
choices: As low as it goes, behind your neck
Removed for comfort on long drives
Tilted away so it does not touch your head
Directly behind the back of your head, not down at your neck
explanation: Head restraints help prevent whiplash, especially when you are hit from behind. Set it so it sits right behind the back of your head; one that is too low gives little protection.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 9, MT p. 29, AZ p. 20, PA p. 36)

prompt: How should the side mirrors be set?
choices: So the side of your car fills most of the mirror
So that when you lean toward that side, you can just barely see the side of your car
Aimed down at the rear tires
Folded in to reduce wind noise
explanation: Set side mirrors so you barely see the side of your vehicle when you lean toward that side. This shows more of the lane next to you and reduces blind spots.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 35, CO p. 9)

prompt: Why should heavy loose items like backpacks or tools be secured or put in the trunk?
choices: They make the car use much more fuel
In a sudden stop or crash they keep moving and can hit people
They can set off the airbags
They can block the radio signal
explanation: Loose items become projectiles in a crash, traveling at the speed the car was moving. Put heavy objects in the trunk or secure them.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 35, NY p. 49)

prompt: Why is a water bottle rolling around on the driver's floor dangerous?
choices: It may freeze in winter
It mainly distracts passengers
It can damage the floor mats
It can roll under the brake or gas pedal and keep you from using it
explanation: Objects on the floor can roll under the brake pedal or accelerator and interfere with your ability to slow or stop. Clear the driver's floor before you drive.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 9, MT p. 29)

prompt: In an emergency stop in a car with anti-lock brakes (ABS), how should you brake?
choices: Press hard and keep firm, steady pressure on the pedal
Pump the pedal rapidly
Press gently and release over and over
Pull the parking brake
explanation: With ABS, apply firm and continuous pressure and do not pump the brakes. ABS only works while you keep the pedal pressed.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 65, NH p. 40, CO p. 28)

prompt: During a hard stop, your ABS-equipped car's brake pedal vibrates and you hear a clicking noise. What should you do?
choices: Lift your foot because the brakes are failing
Start pumping the brake pedal
Keep firm pressure on the pedal; this is the ABS working normally
Shift into neutral
explanation: A vibrating or pushing-back pedal and mechanical noises are normal when ABS is working. Do not let up on the pedal or pump it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., NH p. 40, PA p. 65, CO p. 28)

prompt: What is a key advantage of anti-lock brakes (ABS) in an emergency?
choices: You can safely follow other cars more closely
It keeps working even after you take your foot off the brake
It lets you brake later before every curve
You can keep steering while braking hard because the wheels do not lock
explanation: ABS keeps the wheels from locking, so you can stop without skidding and still steer around a hazard. It is not a reason to follow closely, and it only works while you hold the pedal down.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CO p. 28-29, NH p. 40)

prompt: When should you NOT use cruise control?
choices: On a dry, flat highway with light traffic
On wet, icy, or snowy roads
On a long, straight interstate in clear weather
When you want to save fuel on a dry highway
explanation: Do not use cruise control on slippery roads. You need full control of the accelerator in rain, snow and ice.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 45, CO p. 19, NE p. 70)

prompt: Why is cruise control dangerous on a slippery road?
choices: It turns off the anti-lock brakes
It locks the steering wheel straight
If the wheels start to spin, cruise control keeps applying power when you need to reduce it
It can only hold speeds above 70 mph
explanation: To stop wheel spin and regain control, you must reduce power. An active cruise control keeps applying power, which keeps the wheels spinning.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 45)

prompt: Why is carbon monoxide from a car's exhaust especially dangerous?
choices: It is a deadly gas that you cannot see or smell
It has a strong smell that warns you right away
It is only produced by diesel engines
It is only harmful in very hot weather
explanation: All gas-powered vehicles produce carbon monoxide, a deadly, colorless and odorless gas. You cannot smell it, so you may not know you are breathing it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 77, PA p. 99, TX p. 74)

prompt: It is freezing outside and you want to warm up your car, which is parked in an attached garage. What is the safe way?
choices: Open the garage door fully before starting the engine, or back the car outside
Keep the garage door closed so the heat stays in
Open the garage door a few inches
Keep the car windows up while it runs in the garage
explanation: Never run your engine in a closed or partly closed garage. Carbon monoxide builds up quickly and can kill.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 99, CA p. 77, TX p. 74)

prompt: You are stuck in deep snow and will wait in the car with the engine running for heat. What is most important?
choices: Keep all the windows tightly closed to hold in heat
Run the engine at high idle without stopping
Keep the tailpipe clear of snow and open a window slightly
Cover the tailpipe to keep snow out
explanation: A tailpipe blocked by snow can push carbon monoxide into the car. Clear the tailpipe and partly open a window whenever you sit in an idling vehicle.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., PA p. 99, TX p. 74)

prompt: Which group of symptoms can signal carbon monoxide poisoning in a vehicle?
choices: Sneezing, itchy eyes, and a runny nose
Headache, dizziness, drowsiness, and nausea
A sudden burst of energy and alertness
Sore muscles in your legs and back
explanation: Carbon monoxide poisoning can cause tiredness, yawning, dizziness, headache, nausea and confusion. If you notice these, get fresh air and have the exhaust system checked.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., CA p. 77, PA p. 99)

prompt: A passenger becomes dizzy and confused after sitting in an idling car, and you suspect carbon monoxide. What should you do first?
choices: Turn up the heater and keep them in the car
Give them coffee and let them rest in the back seat
Close the windows and drive them home
Get them out into fresh air and call 911
explanation: Move a carbon monoxide victim to fresh air right away and call 911 or seek emergency medical care.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g., TX p. 74, PA p. 99)
